title: Wu Qi and the Soldier's Wound
text:
Wu Qi was a famous general of the Warring States period in China, who served the states of Lu, Wei and Chu around the late fifth and early fourth centuries BC. Sima Qian describes his way of commanding.

As a general, Wu Qi ate and dressed the same as the lowest-ranking soldiers. When he slept he did not use a mat. On the march he did not ride, and he carried his own rations. He shared all the hardships of his men.

Once a soldier had an abscess, and Wu Qi himself sucked out the pus. When the soldier's mother heard about it, she wept. Someone asked her why she was crying, since her son was only a soldier and the general himself had sucked his wound.

She answered that years before, Wu Qi had done the same for her son's father. Her husband had followed him into battle without ever turning back, and had died at the hands of the enemy. Now that the general had sucked her son's wound, she said, she did not know where her son would die. That was why she wept.
lesson: Care for your people because it is right, and be honest with yourself about what loyalty you are asking for in return.
source: Sima Qian, Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian), chapter 65
